title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 8: The Moot Court — a Virtual Legal Reality
keywords: Association of Law Students of the Philippines
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- remarks at the finals of the First National Moot Court Competition, sponsored as the centerpiece of the second year of the Supreme Court's centennial celebrations under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman.'

CJP explained why the moot court goes beyond the National Speech Festival that preceded it: where debates and oratory develop eloquence, the moot court targets the specific skills of a great lawyer -- research, pleading preparation, knowledge of law, mastery of specific facts, teamwork and advocacy.

He characterized the competition as the nearest thing to actual appellate practice and as a form of virtual legal reality: the facts are hypothetical but the issues, arguments and authorities are real, the judges at each level are real judges and justices, and nothing is scripted.

He closed with extensive acknowledgements of the subcommittee, brief graders, regional organizers, appellate and Supreme Court judges and the author of the hypothetical DNA case, and expressed the hope that the competition would be held annually and eventually written into law school curricula under the reform program.
sub_topics: The centenary frame: the Court's 100th birthday on June 11, 2001, a Centenary Executive Committee appointed to mark it, and more than fifty projects under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman,' emphasizing allegiance to one cause, justice, and to one entity, the nation.
The reach of the celebrations across intellectual, cultural, historical, educational, physical and structural activities in all regions and sectors.
The two goals of the celebrations: to communicate the judiciary's role in nation building, and to focus on and encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program.

The extension of the originally one-year celebrations to June 11, 2002, with the National Speech Festival -- oratory, debate and essay -- as the major activity of the first year and the National Moot Court Competition as the centerpiece of the second.

The contrast between the two: the Speech Festival promoted forensic competition and mastery of language, while the moot court seeks the specific skills needed by a great lawyer and goes beyond mere eloquence or rhetoric.

What makes a moot court different from debate or oratory: live, active and unrehearsed interaction between contending speakers and judges, so that the contest runs between the mooters and the judges as well as among the mooters, with the magistrates themselves judged on preparation, expertise and readiness to ask relevant questions.

The competition's national structure: elimination rounds in law schools across the regions, regional winners meeting in the quarterfinal and semifinal rounds, and two finalists vying for the national championship.

The graduated bench: full-blooded regional trial court judges in the regional rounds, carefully chosen Court of Appeals justices in the national rounds, and incumbent and retired Supreme Court justices in the final match.

Virtual legal reality without a script: everything arranged to give a real and authentic feel, yet with no drama or movie's script, so participants must rely on their own resourcefulness, preparation and skill in largely unrehearsed and extemporaneous proceedings.

Thanks to the National Moot Court Subcommittee headed by Dean and Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Merlin M. Magallona, with members drawn from the Philippine Association of Law Professors, the Philippine Judges Association, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, the Philippine Bar Association, the Philippine Lawyers Association, the Philippine Association of Law Schools, the UP Law Center, the Centenary Execom and the Association of Law Students of the Philippines.

Acknowledgement of the magistrates and deans who reviewed and graded the written briefs, of the executive judges and IBP chapter presidents who ran the regional preliminaries from Manila and Quezon City to Baguio, San Pablo, Iloilo, Cebu, Davao and Cagayan de Oro, and of the twenty Court of Appeals justices who served in the quarterfinal and semifinal rounds.

Recognition of the Supreme Court magistrates who sat as the 'High Tribunal' for the finals, with Justice Vicente V. Mendoza acting as chief justice, and of former UP Law Dean Pacifico Agabin for authoring the hypothetical DNA case on which the whole program revolved.

The closing hope that the Philippine Association of Law Schools and the Association of Law Students of the Philippines would continue the competition annually, and that law schools would make the moot court a regular part of their improved curricula pursuant to the reform program.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced Justice Panganiban's remarks at the finals of the First National Moot Court Competition. He set the occasion in its centenary frame: the Supreme Court had celebrated its 100th birthday on June 11, 2001 and had appointed a Centenary Executive Committee that lined up more than fifty projects under the theme 'Katarungan at Bayan, Magpakailanman,' emphasizing allegiance to one cause, justice, and to one entity, the nation. The celebrations, he said, ran across intellectual, cultural, historical, educational, physical and structural activities in all regions, with two goals: to communicate the judiciary's role in nation building and to encourage participation in the ongoing judicial reform program. Originally scheduled for one year, they had been extended to June 11, 2002; the National Speech Festival, comprising oratorical, debate and essay contests, had been the major activity of the first year, and the moot court was the centerpiece of the second. He distinguished the two. The speech festival promoted forensic competition and mastery of language, but the moot court had more specific objectives and went beyond mere eloquence or rhetoric, seeking to enhance research, pleading preparation, knowledge of law, mastery of specific facts, teamwork and advocacy. Unlike debates and oratories, he explained, moot courts involve live, unrehearsed interaction between the speakers and the judges, so that the magistrates are themselves judged on their preparation, expertise and readiness to ask relevant questions. The contest was national in scope, with school eliminations, regional winners meeting in quarterfinals and semifinals, and two finalists competing for the championship; regional trial court judges sat in the regional rounds, Court of Appeals justices in the national rounds, and incumbent and retired Supreme Court justices in the final. He called it the nearest thing to actual appellate practice -- a virtual legal reality in which the facts are hypothetical but the issues, arguments and authorities are real, and which, being neither a drama nor a movie, has no script. He thanked the subcommittee under Merlin M. Magallona, the brief graders, the regional organizers, the twenty appellate justices, the simulated High Tribunal under Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, and Dean Pacifico Agabin for authoring the hypothetical DNA case, and hoped the contest would continue annually and enter law school curricula.
